name: 3DO
tierWhy: The 3DO Company sold its assets at a bankruptcy auction on August 14, 2003 and nothing is sold under the 3DO name today, but the name is still held and fought over: in July 2026 two unrelated firms each claimed a 3DO trademark, and a third sells games the company once owned.[^16][^35][^33]

place: Game console standard, then game publisher · Redwood City, California
title: 3DO (1991–2003): the $699 console and Army Men
description: 3DO designed a $699 game console that others built, licensed its next design for $100 million, published Army Men and filed for Chapter 11 in 2003.

card.blurb: Trip Hawkins designed a console and let other companies build it and price it. It launched at $699. A decade and one reinvention later, everything 3DO owned sold for $4.6 million.

stat.label: raised when every game and patent was auctioned

hero.dates: Began operations Oct 1991. Console launched Oct 1993. Chapter 11 on May 28, 2003.
hero.standfirst: 3DO failed twice: first as the company that would set the standard for every living-room machine, then as the publisher of little green plastic soldiers.
hero.deck: The 3DO Company designed a game console for other firms to build and sell, and ended as a game publisher that filed for Chapter 11 in May 2003. It licensed the design to Matsushita, Goldstar and others, and planned to live on a royalty from every disc. The machine reached stores in October 1993 at $699 with almost nothing to play. Three years later 3DO sold its next-generation design for $100 million, became a game publisher and had one profitable year on the back of Army Men. The figures come from the company’s [10-K, 10-Q and 8-K filings](#sources) on SEC EDGAR, The New York Times, the Los Angeles Times and trade coverage of the period.

findings.title: It set the price of nothing it sold.
findings.text: 3DO licensed the design and collected royalties; Matsushita built the machine and priced it at $699. Hawkins said in 1996: “we had all our eggs in one basket, and we didn’t have control of the basket.”[^20][^25]

findings.title: The hardware made money only when it was sold off.
findings.text: 3DO lost $150.5M (derived) from its start to March 1996. Its only large profits, in fiscal 1997 and 1998, came from Matsushita’s $100M license fee and a $20M sale to Samsung.[^1][^3][^4]

findings.title: The second company depended on three brands.
findings.text: In fiscal 1999 Army Men, BattleTanx and Might and Magic made up about 75% of revenue.[^4] Revenue peaked at $122.2M in fiscal 2000 and fell to $53.7M two years later.[^5][^7]

findings.title: The founder was the lender of last resort.
findings.text: Trip Hawkins lent the company $3M in October 2002 and agreed to lend up to $8M that December. It filed for Chapter 11 five months later.[^10][^11][^14]

findings.title: The name outlived the assets.
findings.text: The games went to seven bidders in 2003. In 2026 two firms were still disputing who owns the 3DO trademark.[^16][^35]
